questions.title: Does a 'partial stay' of a preliminary injunction mean the lower court's order remains effective for the non-stayed portions, or is the entire injunction voided until the appellate court rules?
questions.question_body: I'm reading *Pacito v. Trump* and the Ninth Circuit says they are staying the district court's preliminary injunctions "in their entirety except as specified." However, they explicitly carve out an exception where they direct the government to reinstate cooperative agreements for existing refugees. If the appellate court stays an injunction, doesn't that usually freeze everything? How can the district court's order still be partially operative (regarding reinstatement) while being stayed otherwise? Is this a unique procedural mechanism for mixed rulings on statutory vs. constitutional claims?

questions.title: How does 8 U.S.C. § 1522 reconcile 'authorization' language with mandatory duties when Congress appropriates specific funds for refugee services?
questions.question_body: Judge Lee's dissent argues that because § 1522 is titled "Authorization" and uses phrases like "is authorized," it gives the Executive Branch discretion not to fund refugee resettlement. However, the majority points to subsections using "shall" (e.g., "shall... make available sufficient resources") and notes that Congress appropriated billions for this purpose. In statutory interpretation, does a section titled "Authorization" automatically override explicit "shall" mandates found within that same section, especially when specific appropriations exist? Does the phrase "to the extent of available appropriations" turn a mandatory duty into a conditional one?

questions.title: Can an appellate court grant a stay based on likelihood of success on statutory grounds while simultaneously denying relief on constitutional/INA grounds without issuing a full opinion yet?
questions.question_body: The panel orders states they are granting a stay because the government is likely to succeed on challenging the suspension of admissions (citing *Trump v. Hawaii*), but they deny a full stay because the government might lose on the APA/statutory claim regarding resettlement services (§ 1522). They admit an opinion on merits will come later. Procedurally, how can they weigh these conflicting likelihood-of-success determinations to issue a narrow stay? Do they essentially split their decision-making process between two distinct legal theories before fully briefing either?

questions.title: What is the legal distinction between terminating 'cooperative agreements' versus suspending 'funding,' and why does it matter for standing under the APA?
questions.question_body: The background mentions that after Feb 25, the government terminated cooperative agreements with NGOs, even though they claimed to be just suspending funding. Later, Judge Lee argues about whether § 1522 mandates funding or just authorizes it. Why did the plaintiffs sue under both the Refugee Act and the APA? Specifically, if Congress didn't *mandate* funding (as Lee suggests), does terminating a contract violate any statute if no money was technically promised in perpetuity? Or is the violation purely procedural under APA because they changed policy without notice/comment?

questions.title: If Congress reduces appropriations via a Rescissions Act, does that trigger an automatic exemption from statutory mandates like 8 U.S.C. § 1522(a)?
questions.question_body: The opinion notes that Congress appropriated $3.178 billion but then passed a Rescissions Act reducing it by $800 million. The majority cites § 1522(a)'s phrase "to the extent of available appropriations." If Congress cuts funds specifically targeting these programs, does that legally excuse the Executive Branch from complying with mandatory directives like making cash assistance available or providing medical services? Or does "available appropriations" refer only to funds currently in existence at any given moment, meaning if funds are rescinded mid-year, the mandate simply becomes impossible to fulfill rather than optional?

questions.title: Does *Nken v. Holder*'s four-factor test allow an appellate court to balance irreparable harm differently for different classes of plaintiffs within a single case?
questions.question_body: In previous orders mentioned in this text (March/April/May), the panel carved out exceptions for people already conditionally approved before Jan 20. Now in this September order, they seem to be balancing harm differently again: allowing suspension of new entries but mandating service for current residents. How does *Nken* handle cases where one group suffers irreparable harm (new entrants blocked) while another group suffers financial/administrative harm (existing refugees losing services)? Can a court find irreparable harm exists for Group A but not Group B in a single consolidated appeal?
